items.text: Gold dug from a mine
items.rationale: Mining moves gold out of the ground but does not change it into a new substance, so it is a natural resource.

items.text: Fish oil
items.rationale: Fish oil is harvested from living things, and extracting it does not make a new substance, so it is a natural resource.

items.text: Crude oil pumped from underground

items.text: Nitrogen gas collected from the air
items.rationale: Gases taken from the air are natural resources; collecting them does not change what they are.

items.text: Polyester fabric
items.rationale: Polyester is made by chemical processes from substances taken out of petroleum, so it is synthetic.

items.text: PLA plastic pellets
items.rationale: Corn is the natural resource; a series of chemical reactions turns it into the new substance PLA.

items.text: Sucralose sweetener

questions.explanation: Natural resources come from nature; digging, pumping or harvesting them does not turn them into new substances. Synthetic materials are new materials made when chemical processes change those resources. Crude oil is natural; the polyester made from it is synthetic.

choices.text: Its properties fit the product's needs, within cost and other limits.
choices.rationale: Correct: synthetic materials can be engineered to have the properties a product requires, and the choice must still fit the budget and other constraints.

choices.rationale: Nothing makes synthetic materials automatically cheaper. Cost depends on the material, the process and the price of the starting resources, so it has to be checked for each design. Cost is a constraint to check, not a guarantee.

choices.text: Being made in a lab proves that a material is safe to use.

choices.text: It can be made without using up Earth's natural resources.

questions.explanation: Engineers start with what a product must do and the limits they must work within. A synthetic material can be designed to have the needed properties, such as strength with flexibility or sweetness without calories. It still has to fit the budget and other constraints, and it still comes from natural resources.
questions.misconception: Engineers pick synthetic materials because 'synthetic' is automatically cheaper, safer or free of natural resources.

questions.prompt: Table salt, table sugar and the sweetener sucralose can all be food additives. What makes a substance a food additive?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Table salt, table sugar and the sweetener sucralose can all be food additives. What makes a substance a food additive?

choices.text: It is added on purpose to improve a food, such as its flavor.
choices.rationale: Correct: a food additive is defined by its job. It is put into food on purpose to improve its flavor, color, freshness, nutrition or safety.

choices.text: It is made in a factory from substances that come from petroleum.
choices.rationale: Salt and sugar are food additives that come from nature. Some additives are made from petroleum, but where a substance comes from does not decide whether it is an additive.

choices.text: It has no calories, so it can stand in for sugar in a food.
choices.rationale: Sugar is itself a food additive, and it has plenty of calories. Zero-calorie sweeteners are only one kind of additive.

choices.text: It is a chemical, while foods straight from nature have none.
choices.rationale: Every food is made of chemical substances. Being a chemical does not make something an additive; being added to food for a purpose does.

questions.explanation: A food additive is defined by its job: it is added to food on purpose to improve its flavor, color, freshness, nutrition or safety. Additives can be natural, like salt and sugar, or synthetic, like sucralose. Whether an additive is a good choice depends on evidence about that substance, not on whether it is natural or synthetic.
questions.misconception: Food additives are always artificial chemicals, or they are always calorie-free.
questions.hint: Look back at the three examples. Which choices would rule out at least one of them?

evidence.supports: A food additive is any substance added to food to improve its flavor, color, freshness, nutritional value or safety.
Table salt and table sugar are natural substances that are also used as food additives; many other additives, such as the zero-calorie sweetener sucralose, are synthetic.

questions.prompt: In the 1960s and 1970s, scientists searched through U.S. plants for substances that might fight cancer, and they found paclitaxel in Pacific yew bark. Why do researchers often look to nature first for new medicines?
questions.accessiblePrompt: In the 1960s and 1970s, scientists searched through United States plants for substances that might fight cancer, and they found paclitaxel in Pacific yew bark. Why do researchers often look to nature first for new medicines?

choices.text: Many medicines were first found in substances made by living things.
choices.rationale: Correct: living things make a huge variety of substances. Penicillin comes from a mold and paclitaxel was found in yew bark, so nature is a good place to start looking.

choices.text: Substances from nature are safe, so they can skip safety testing.
choices.rationale: Natural does not mean safe. Every possible medicine, natural or not, has to be tested for safety and for whether it works.

choices.text: Medicines cannot be made in a lab by chemical reactions.
choices.rationale: Many drugs are made by chemical reactions, some starting from substances in petroleum. Looking to nature is a good first step, not the only way.

choices.text: Taking a substance from nature costs less than making one in a laboratory.
choices.rationale: Not necessarily. Paclitaxel made from yew bark was very expensive, and stripping the bark killed slow-growing trees.

questions.explanation: Living things make a huge variety of substances, and many medicines were first discovered in them: penicillin comes from a mold, and paclitaxel was found during a survey of plants. That track record is why researchers often search nature first. Every substance found this way still has to be tested, and chemists often find better ways to make it.
questions.misconception: Medicines from nature are automatically safe, or medicines can only be made in a lab.
questions.hint: Check each choice against the lesson's medicine examples, such as penicillin and paclitaxel.

questions.prompt: PLA and a plastic made from ethylene, a substance in petroleum, are both made of long chain molecules. In a hot composting facility, PLA breaks down within months, but the ethylene plastic lasts for years. What best explains the difference?
questions.accessiblePrompt: P L A and a plastic made from ethylene, a substance in petroleum, are both made of long chain molecules. In a hot composting facility, P L A breaks down within months, but the ethylene plastic lasts for years. What best explains the difference?

choices.text: PLA came from corn, and anything made from plants breaks down quickly.
choices.rationale: Where a plastic comes from doesn't decide this: some plant-based plastics don't biodegrade, and certain petroleum-based ones can. What matters is how the molecules are built.

choices.text: PLA's atoms are softer, so bacteria can chew right through them.
choices.rationale: Single atoms aren't soft or hard; those are properties of a whole material. Breakdown depends on which bonds join the units in the chains.

choices.text: Their chains are built from different units, and PLA's are easier to break down.
choices.rationale: Correct: PLA's chains are made from units joined by bonds that heat, water and microbes in compost can split. The ethylene plastic's chains resist this, so it lasts for years.

choices.text: The ethylene plastic is synthetic, and living things can't break down synthetic materials.
choices.rationale: PLA is synthetic too: it is made from corn by chemical reactions. Being synthetic doesn't decide whether a material breaks down; the structure of its molecules does.

questions.explanation: A material's properties come from how its molecules are built, not from where the material came from. PLA and plastics made from ethylene both have long chains, but the chains are built from different units joined in different ways. In hot, moist compost, PLA's chains can be split and then digested by microbes, while the ethylene plastic's chains hold up for years.
questions.misconception: Whether a material breaks down depends on where it came from or on a 'synthetic' label, not on how its molecules are built.
questions.hint: Some plastics made from plants don't break down in compost, and a few made from petroleum do. So what must matter instead?

evidence.locator: Section 1, synthetic material and PLA paragraphs
evidence.supports: The structure and composition of a synthetic material's molecules give it its useful properties; PLA, made from corn, is a polymer of long chains.
Many plastics are made from ethylene, a substance separated from petroleum, and are polymers made of long chains.
Traditional plastic lasts so long that once it is buried in a landfill it remains there for years.
PLA contains molecules that bacteria can break down, but it needs a heated facility to break down in a timely way.
PLA is made from corn through a series of chemical reactions.

evidence.title: Bioplastics: a better option for the environment? (FOR349)
evidence.supports: Bio-based plastics are not necessarily biodegradable, and certain petroleum-based plastics can biodegrade; PLA readily breaks down only in a commercial composting facility with high heat, water and air, not in the environment or a backyard compost pile.

evidence.title: Recent advances in high performance poly(lactide): from "green" plasticization to super-tough materials via (reactive) compounding (Kfoury et al., 2013)
evidence.supports: PLA is a poly(lactic acid) polyester derived from renewable resources, with lactide as its main monomer; aliphatic polyesters are hydrolytically degradable because their backbones contain water-sensitive ester bonds.

questions.conditions: Both plastics are kept in the same hot, moist industrial composting facility.
questions.limitations: Simplified: in compost, heat and water first split PLA's chains into shorter pieces, and microbes then digest the pieces. Not every plastic made from plants breaks down in compost.
